summary: For 7–8 year olds, teach the non-negotiable safety rule that you must NEVER look directly at the Sun — even through sunglasses, even on a cloudy day — paired with a simple, age-appropriate reason (the Sun is so bright it can permanently damage the light-sensitive cells inside the eye). Lead by surfacing then directly refuting the central misconception that sunglasses or cloud make it safe to stare. Separately build the 'ways to protect' half of the objective: naming eye protections (sunglasses for general brightness/glare, shade, hat, and safe indirect viewing via a pinhole/box projector) distinct from skin protections (sunscreen, clothing, shade, hat), and optionally testing which sunglasses block the most UV using UV-sensitive beads — while stressing that blocking UV is not the same as making direct viewing safe. The focusing/retinal optics is teacher background; the pupil expectation is the rule, a simple cause, and named protections.
misconceptions: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day (cloud removes the danger).
Wearing sunglasses (or 'dark enough' glasses) makes it safe to look directly at the Sun.
The Sun is only dangerous on hot/bright summer days.
If it doesn't feel hot or look painfully bright, the Sun isn't harmful to the eyes.
Only some skin tones need protection from UV, rather than everyone.
Sunglasses protect the eyes the same way for staring as for general brightness (conflating UV protection with safe direct viewing).

activities.title: The Sun-and-eye safety scene: naming the 'but I've got sunglasses' excuse
steps: Look at an illustration of a child outdoors under the Sun and predict aloud or in writing: 'Is it ever safe to look straight at the Sun?'
Reveal the Sun-to-eye path: light gathers through the eye's lens to a tiny point inside the eye — caption 'the Sun can damage the inside of your eye for ever — never look straight at it.'
Reveal the sunglasses flap after stating your own thought 'but I've got sunglasses': 'sunglasses dim the brightness and block some UV — but they do NOT make it safe to stare at the Sun.'
Reveal the cloud: 'still not safe on a cloudy day — the Sun is still dangerously bright through thin cloud or haze.'

Reveal the pinhole/box projector: the safe way to watch the Sun is by looking at its projected image on a surface, never at the Sun itself and never by holding anything up to your eyes toward the Sun.
activities.insight: Looking directly at the Sun is never safe, and the common reasons children think it becomes safe — such as wearing sunglasses or the Sun looking dim behind cloud — are each wrong; there is a separate safe way to observe the Sun indirectly.

activities.title: UV-bead fair test: which sunglasses block the most UV?
steps: Set out UV-sensitive beads and watch THE BEADS change colour in sunlight (or a UV source) — keep your eyes on the beads, never on the Sun.

Using fresh beads that have been kept out of sunlight (not the beads already coloured in the first step), put a matching set of beads under each pair of sunglasses (or under clear plastic spread with sun cream), plus one uncovered set to compare. Lay them out side by side in the same light at the same time, keeping everything else the same, and observe how much each set changes colour.
Record which item lets the beads change least, i.e. which blocks the most UV, and discuss what makes this a fair test (same beads, same light, change only the sunglasses).
State explicitly: blocking the most UV is NOT the same as making it safe to look straight at the Sun.
activities.insight: There are testable, evidence-based 'ways to protect' — the test can show whether some sunglasses block more UV than others (and how dark a lens looks does not tell you how much UV it blocks) — but blocking UV helps protect eyes from UV exposure and does not permit staring at the Sun.

activities.title: Eyes vs skin: sorting protections and checking the rule
steps: Sort protection actions into 'protects eyes' (sunglasses, never staring, safe indirect viewing) and 'protects skin' (sunscreen, clothing); note that 'shade' and 'a sun hat' are shared items that belong in BOTH groups, so this sort allows an item to go in two places.
Answer short check questions: Is it safe to look at the Sun while wearing sunglasses? (No.) Is it safe on a cloudy day? (No.)
State the rule in your own words and give one simple reason, then name at least two ways to protect your eyes outside on a very bright day.
Discuss the torch question: why is a quick glance at a torch different from a glance at the Sun?
activities.insight: Eye protection and skin protection meet different needs (with shade and a sun hat helping both); the Sun is far more intense than any ordinary household light, so we must never look directly at it, whereas a quick accidental glance at an ordinary torch is unlikely to harm your eyes (though we still should not stare into torches).

activities.title: Ask the eye doctor: why can't I look at the Sun?
steps: Pose a child's questions to an optometrist/eye-doctor persona: 'Why can't I look at the Sun?' and 'What if I wear sunglasses?'

Hear the authoritative answer: the Sun is so intensely bright it can permanently damage the light-sensitive cells inside the eye; sunglasses reduce glare but do not make looking safe; instruments like binoculars or telescopes make it far worse.
Repeat the rule back in your own words and name the safe indirect way to watch the Sun (looking at its projected image on a surface, never directly).
activities.insight: An expert confirms the same single rule and reason, reinforcing that there are no exceptions and that instruments increase the danger.

checkQuestion: Your friend puts on dark sunglasses and says 'Now it's safe for me to look straight at the sun.' Is your friend right? Explain what you would tell them.
checkAnswer: No. Sunglasses cut down brightness and glare, but they do NOT make it safe to look straight at the sun — you should never look directly at it, because the sun is so intensely bright it can permanently damage your eyes even through sunglasses. Protect your eyes with shade, a hat, and by not looking at it.
